title: Fasting days (Didache 8)
hook: fast on Wednesdays and Fridays, and pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day
tomorrow: where would you look for a sermon with no words in it?

segments.voice: Scattered grain on the hills, gathered into one loaf: the Didache's prayer at the table. Scattered, then one loaf. The same little book has a calendar in it too.
screen: `SCATTERED, THEN ONE LOAF.` → `A CALENDAR IN THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: Sunday night, a phone on the kitchen counter. Someone is setting up the week. Two days get a small circle: Wednesday, Friday. Three alarms go in, every day, each with the same one-word label: pause. A roommate glances over and guesses a medicine schedule. It isn't. It's a rhythm out of a short book that churches have handed down, and it fits on one screen.
screen: `TWO DAYS CIRCLED.` → `THREE ALARMS: PAUSE.` → `A MEDICINE SCHEDULE?`

segments.voice: The book is the Didache, and chapter eight is short and practical. Fast, it says, on the fourth day and on the day of Preparation: Wednesday and Friday. Then it turns to prayer. Pray as the Lord commanded in his Gospel, it says, and it writes out the Lord's Prayer, the one Jesus teaches in Matthew: "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name." The Didache's version ends in praise: for yours is the power and the glory forever. Then the instruction: pray this three times a day. That rhythm has older roots. In the book of Daniel, the prophet "kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God." A psalm says, "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray." The Didache takes that old rhythm and sets the Lord's Prayer inside it. What strikes some readers is how ordinary it all is. Two days a week with less food. Three short pauses a day. A faith with a calendar and a clock, built into weeks that otherwise look like anyone else's. Nothing here asks for a mountaintop. It asks for Wednesday.
screen: `WEDNESDAY AND FRIDAY.` · `THE LORD'S PRAYER, WRITTEN OUT.` · `DANIEL KNEELS THREE TIMES.` · `A CALENDAR AND A CLOCK.` · then, large: `THREE TIMES A DAY.`

segments.voice: Turn your phone face down and slide it out of reach for the length of the sit: a small fast, right now. If a Wednesday fast appeals to you, choose only what's safe for your body, a snack, a coffee, your phone at lunch; anyone who shouldn't skip food can fast from something else.
Fasting days. Wednesday and Friday in the Didache, kept beside the Lord's Prayer, prayed three times a day.
Your line: three times a day. Evening, morning and noon, the same short prayer. Rest well.

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3 (story shape: a phone calendar set up on a Sunday night). Title, word, carry and sources kept.

Didache 8:1 contrasts its fasting days with those of 'the hypocrites' (who fast on Monday and Thursday). The script leaves this out on purpose, so no other community is cast as a foil, and makes no claim that the Didache gives no reason. A Keeper may decide whether and how to mention it.
The Didache's doxology ('for yours is the power and the glory forever') is paraphrased; no manuscript claim is made about Matthew's ending.

The practice, the chat and the fork all keep fasting small and safe; the practice gives an alternative for anyone who shouldn't skip food. Grace is a teenager; the chat's right answer steers her to a non-food fast before choir. Keep this.
howItsDone: 'some Christians still keep Wednesday and Friday' (e.g. Orthodox practice) is kept general; confirm.
Gloss 'Preparation' as the day before the Sabbath, Friday; confirm.
